This brom of the week is coming a little late, but whatever, this subverse is as lively as the last picture. Like the pineapple, this is one of those bromeliads that has probably been right under your nose for many years without you knowing about it, especially if you live in the south of the US. While it doesn't grow wild around me, it's in greenhouses and potting arrangements almost everywhere I turn. The stuff is prolific to say the very least. Finding where one individual specimen ends and the next begins is an exercise in futility as they multiply rapidly in every which direction and usually do not break away from the parent. While it isn't a parasite, it can hinder the growth of the hosting tree by blocking sunlight and can cause damage that wouldn't occur otherwise in high winds due to the increased mass. A very inconspicuous bromeliad, right down to their tiny flowers.

  • Introduced to Hawaii in the 19th century, became known as "Pele's hair," and often used in leis.

  • Uses " including building insulation, mulch, packing material, mattress stuffing, and fiber."

  • A true epiphyte, clumping in large colonies on trees and relying on trichomes to absorb moisture and nutrients

  • "One species of spider, Pelegrina tillandsiae , makes Spanish Moss its sole habitat."
